PDHS 1990-91 (KR: 6,428 children) and PDHS 2017-18 (KR: 12,708 children) -- NCHS/1978 reference for both years -- All figures DHS sample-weighted

Child Stunting Analysis -- Pakistan 1991 to 2018

Stunting = height-for-age z-score (HAZ) < −2 standard deviations using NCHS/1978 reference (hw5) applied to BOTH years for direct comparability. Socioeconomic classification: asset-based wealth quintile constructed from 9 common items available in both surveys (electricity, TV, fridge, motorcycle, car, flush toilet, piped water, pucca wall, pucca roof). Mother and father education directly comparable — identical DHS v106/v701 coding.

HIES 2024-25 Sec 6a microdata · n=30,102 households · Section 110xxx eating-out codes · All figures CPI-adjusted where applicable

Modern Pakistan - How the country is eating, spending, connecting

For the first time, HIES 2024-25 separately codes Pizza, Burger & Shwarma (ITC 110013), Buffet & High Tea (110020), and Coffee/Tea out of home (110006/110019). The data reveals a consumption shift that aggregate food spending misses entirely. 70% of Pakistani households now eat out. 31.5% spend on fast food. Urban families spend more on eating out than on home groceries.

PDHS 1990-91 (n=6,393) · PDHS 2017-18 (n=14,502) · Cross-validated against 5 household surveys · DHS-weighted · v505 = number of other wives

Polygamy in Pakistan — 1991 vs 2018 · Six-Survey Cross-Validation

Direct PDHS self-report: 3.71% of currently married women (15-49) are in polygamous unions (2018). Household roster method across 5 surveys gives 1.07-1.43% — lower because rosters only capture co-resident wives. Both methods consistently show Balochistan highest, Punjab lowest. National rate barely changed in 27 years despite major provincial shifts.

LFS 2024-25 n=98,807 children 5-16 · PSLM 2004-05 · PSLM 2015-16 · HIES 2024-25 · PBS 2023 population base 47.3M children 5-16

Out-of-School Children in Pakistan — Multi-Survey Analysis 2004-2025

21-32% of Pakistani children aged 5-16 are out of school depending on the definition. Sindh and Balochistan have 3-4x higher out-of-school risk than Punjab in regression. Urban Sindh shows paradoxically higher rates than rural Sindh driven by Karachi informal settlements. A child in Sindh is three times more likely to be out of school than a child in Punjab — after controlling for gender, age, and rural-urban status.

Total Fertility Rate — Pakistan 1991–2025 (Multi-Survey)

TFR declined from 5.4 (1991) to 3.6 (2018) — a 33% drop in 27 years. Recent CWR-based proxies suggest TFR remains near 3.6-4.0 with Balochistan still above 4.5. Cohort fertility (women 40-49) reveals the true historical burden: completed families of 6.5 children in 1991, 5.2 in 2018.

Gallup Pakistan Digital Analytics · Composite Index · 7 Surveys · 1990–2025

Pakistan Human Flourishing Index (HFI)

A composite 0-100 index across 4 pillars - Health, Education & Capabilities, Women's Empowerment, and Living Standards - computed from 7 independent surveys spanning 35 years. Higher = better flourishing. Each pillar equally sub-weighted across its indicators; pillar weights: Health 30%, Education 25%, Women 20%, Living Standards 25%.

Index Methodology & Limitations
Health (30%)
Facility birth attendance, full immunisation 12-23m, antenatal care coverage, under-5 mortality (inverted). Sources: DHS 1990-91, PSLM 2004/2025, LFS/trends.
Education (25%)
National literacy (10+), female literacy, net school enrolment 6-15, female:male literacy ratio. Sources: DHS 1990-91, PSLM 2004/2019/2025, LFS 2018/2024.
Women (20%)
Female literacy, female LFPR (scaled 0-50%), median female marriage age, household decision-making autonomy (2025 only). Sources: All 7 surveys.
Living Standards (25%)
Household electricity, safe/piped water access, connectivity (TV 1990-2004; internet 2019+), food security (100 minus % worried). Methodology note: TV-internet transition creates 2019 break.

Indicators scored 0-100 using linear interpolation between observed floor values and aspirational ceilings (100% for proportions, 10/1000 for mortality, 28yrs for marriage age, 50% for female LFPR). Equal weighting within pillars. Province estimates for 2025 use available PSLM/LFS sub-national data. Missing indicators in earlier years imputed at observed trend. This index is descriptive, not prescriptive.

PSLM 2004-05 · LFS 2005-06 · LFS 2018-19 · LFS 2024-25 · HIES 2024-25 (cross-check) · Youth 15-24

NEET Rate — Youth Not in Employment, Education or Training

NEET fell from 40.7% (2004-05) to 28.8% (2024-25) — a 12pp improvement over two decades. The gender gap remains the dominant driver: female NEET (45.9%) is over 3x the male rate (13.3%) as of 2024-25.

India vs Pakistan — Head-to-Head Comparison

The subcontinent's two largest nations, split at partition in 1947, now on very different demographic paths. India leads on fertility, education, and marital stability — Pakistan holds a narrow edge on marriage age and, unexpectedly, sanitation.
